findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks all existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public SPI loaded via ServiceLoader, and this PR adds a new abstract method `int order()` without a default implementation. Any existing out-of-tree implementation of CryptoProvider (custom crypto provider extensions compiled against the previous keycloak-common) will fail to compile against the new version and, worse, will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when an old jar is used with the new keycloak-common, because CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now calls CryptoProvider::order on every ServiceLoader-discovered provider during sorting. This turns a previously working deployment into one that fails during CryptoIntegration.init. The method should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) so existing implementations keep working.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider (SUN), not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract states this method returns the BouncyCastle security provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the SUN provider on standard JDKs. BouncyIntegration caches the returned provider's name globally (BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) and keycloak-core code uses that name for explicit-provider JCA lookups (e.g., KeyStore/Cipher/Signature.getInstance(alg, BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER)); pinning those lookups to "SUN" will throw NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException for anything SUN does not implement (e.g., PKCS12 keystores, which live in SunJSSE), even though the algorithms are available elsewhere in the JVM. It also needlessly instantiates a KeyStore on every call. The correct behavior for an environment without BouncyCastle is to return null, as WildFlyElytronProvider does.

findings.title: Multiple equal-order providers are now resolved silently and arbitrarily instead of failing fast
findings.body: Previously, having more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath was a hard configuration error ("Multiple crypto providers loaded..."). Now detectProvider sorts by order() descending and silently takes the first, only logging the ignored ones at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so if two server-side providers end up on the classpath together (a real misconfiguration, e.g. both elytron and fips jars present), the winner is determined by ServiceLoader encounter order, which depends on jar/classpath ordering and is effectively arbitrary — the server may run with the wrong crypto provider with no warning above debug level. Equal-order ties should still fail fast, or at least log a warning.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests sign with a P-256 key and never verify the re-encoded DER with JCA
findings.body: The test constructor creates a single key with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, whose default curve is P-256, and reuses it for all three tests. As a result testES384 and testES512 never process real 48-byte or 66-byte r/s values, so the padding/truncation logic in integerToBytes for those sizes is untested despite the test names suggesting otherwise. Additionally, the test only asserts that decode(encode(x)) == x, which is self-consistent by construction; the re-encoded DER signature is never passed to java.security.Signature.verify(), so an encoder bug that produces DER the JCA (or the server) rejects would still pass. Each test should generate a key for the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the re-encoded signature with JCA.
